description: This topic deals with the spatial distribution of people in a region and the change in their numbers over time. It forms a fundamental core of Human Geography and Demography, essential for understanding resource allocation and urban planning.

sections.title: Basic Concepts and Formulas
sections.description: Fundamental definitions and mathematical formulas related to population studies.

key_concepts.explanation: The total number of people living per unit area of land (usually per square kilometer). It represents the man-land ratio.
The change in the size of the population of a specific area between two specific points in time. It can be expressed in absolute numbers or as a percentage, and can be positive or negative.
The difference between the Birth Rate and the Death Rate in a particular region, excluding the effects of in-migration and out-migration.

scientific_principles.application: Used to get a general estimate of overall crowding and spatial distribution of people in a country or region.

scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: Total Population ÷ Total Net Sown Area (Arable Land)
scientific_principles.application: Used to measure the real pressure of the population on the agricultural land available in a country.

sections.title: History of Population Growth in India
sections.description: Crucial phases of Indian demographic history and the timeline of the official Indian Census.

historical_events.significance: Conducted during the tenure of Lord Mayo, but it was non-synchronous and incomplete, covering only parts of the country.
Initiated under Lord Ripon, it marked the beginning of a regular, complete, and synchronous decadal census in India.
The only decade (1911-1921) where India recorded a negative decadal population growth rate (-0.31%) due to severe famines and epidemics like the Spanish Flu.
Marked by a rapid fall in the mortality rate due to improved medical facilities, while the birth rate remained persistently high.

sections.title: Demographic Transition Theory
sections.description: A theory explaining how birth and death rates change as a society transitions from a rural-agrarian economy to an urban-industrial one.

key_concepts.explanation: Characterized by both High Birth Rate and High Death Rate. Population growth is very slow due to epidemics and food shortages (e.g., primitive agrarian tribes).
Birth Rate remains high, but there is a rapid decline in the Death Rate due to improvements in sanitation and healthcare. This leads to a 'Population Explosion' (e.g., developing nations).
Both Birth Rate and Death Rate decline significantly. The population becomes stable or grows very slowly as society becomes urbanized and literate (e.g., developed countries like Japan and Germany).

sections.title: Census of India 2011: Density and Growth Data
sections.description: Vital statistical data regarding the population distribution among Indian States and Union Territories based on the 2011 Census.

geographical_data.key_characteristics: The state with the highest population density in India, with 1,106 persons living per square kilometer.
The state with the lowest population density in India, with only 17 persons living per square kilometer.
The state that recorded the highest decadal population growth rate (27.9%) between 2001 and 2011.
The only Indian state to record a negative decadal population growth rate (-0.6%) during the 2001-2011 period.

important_facts.fact: According to the 2011 Census, the overall average Population Density of India is 382 persons per square kilometer.
The average Decadal Population Growth Rate of India during the 2001-2011 period was 17.64%.
Taking both States and Union Territories into account, Delhi has the highest population density in India (11,320 persons per sq km).

sections.title: Factors Affecting Population Distribution
sections.description: The geographical, economic, and social determinants that influence where people choose to settle across the globe.

key_associations.extra_info: Supports incredibly dense populations due to high agricultural productivity and ease of developing transport networks.
Act as 'pull factors', driving massive rural-to-urban migration by offering better employment, education, and medical facilities.
Despite rugged terrain and dense forests, mining and industrial activities attract significant human settlement and labor migration.
